result.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): A covers the core problems better. It proposes a dry run on recent mail before going live, asks for only the safety caps first and fills in the rest from what it sees, and swaps the bare autonomy number for a plain line saying what that level will and won't do. B handles the slider and the Reply risk well and is better at naming what to keep, but it never proposes previewing actions on real mail. B's later points are also a long run of minor nitpicks, while A is weak on naming what to keep and runs to eight points. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B better covers the main point of the rubric. It proposes a dry run on 30–50 recent emails before going live and says outright that people are asked to decide most when they know least. It also turns the slider and Reply concerns into concrete caps and gives a suggested screen. A has clearer wins on keeping what works, and its 'recommended settings' path is good. But it never proposes previewing what the assistant would do on real mail, and it pads the critique with smaller copy nitpicks.
